title: BRUE Pathway
sources: AAP 2016 Clinical Practice Guideline (Tieder JS et al. Pediatrics 2016;137(5):e20160590)
Merritt JL 2nd, Quinonez RA, Bonkowsky JL, et al. A Framework for Evaluation of the Higher-Risk Infant After a Brief Resolved Unexplained Event. Pediatrics. 2019;144(2):e20184101
Tieder JS, et al. Diagnostic yield of evaluation and CIED/observation for lower-risk BRUE (secondary analyses, 2018-2021)

changelog.change: Built out the higher-risk branch — the risk-elevating features, a targeted feature-matched evaluation (12-lead ECG for all; pertussis, feeding/swallow, non-accidental-trauma workup, EEG, and neuroimaging each gated by specific findings), a not-recommended-routinely list, and a disposition guide — synthesized from the 2019 higher-risk framework (Merritt et al.) plus AAP 2016. Removed the stub callout and needs-primary-source flag. Still guidance, not a validated decision rule.
Initial entry — lower-risk pathway matches AAP 2016 exactly; higher-risk side is a stub pending the 2019 framework.

purpose: Classify an infant event as a BRUE, then stratify lower- vs higher-risk to guide testing and disposition.

body.text: An episode in an infant < 1 year, lasting < 1 minute (typically 20-30 s), with ≥ 1 of: cyanosis or pallor; absent, decreased, or irregular breathing; marked change in tone (hyper- or hypotonia); altered responsiveness — AND no explanation found after a full history and exam. If there is an explanation (e.g. GERD, choking, infection), it is not a BRUE — work up the cause.

items: Gestational age ≥ 32 weeks AND corrected gestational age ≥ 45 weeks
No CPR by a trained medical provider
No concerning history or physical exam findings

body.text: Lower-risk: brief monitoring (continuous pulse oximetry + serial observation), parental education on BRUE and CPR, shared decision-making. Do NOT routinely obtain labs, imaging, admission, or home monitors. May consider a 12-lead ECG and pertussis testing.

There is no validated higher-risk pathway. The 2016 AAP guideline explicitly does not cover these infants; the 2019 framework (Merritt et al.) is expert consensus. Approach: weight the risk-elevating features, do a TARGETED evaluation matched to what is actually concerning, and use shared decision-making about brief admission — not a reflexive shotgun workup.

items: History of prematurity — gestational age < 32 weeks, or corrected age < 45 weeks
More than one event, or events clustered in a short period
Event lasted ≥ 1 minute, or required vigorous stimulation or CPR by a trained provider

Concerning history — family history of sudden unexplained death < 35 years, a prior BRUE/ALTE, a social or safety concern or possible maltreatment, a possible toxic exposure, a clear feeding or positional trigger
Any abnormal physical exam — focal neurologic finding, bruising or other injury, dysmorphism, a pathologic murmur, respiratory distress, or abnormal vital signs

body.text: Targeted evaluation — match the test to the feature

rows: 12-lead ECG (long QT, WPW, cardiomyopathy). Consider a brief period of continuous cardiorespiratory + pulse-oximetry monitoring (observation unit or short admission), especially if age < 2 months, recurrent, or CPR was given.
Color change / apnea + sick contact or incomplete pertussis vaccination
Pertussis PCR; consider a respiratory viral panel (RSV).
Choking, gagging, arching, or a clear feeding association
Feeding / swallowing evaluation. Do NOT routinely start acid suppression or obtain an upper GI series for presumed reflux.
Abnormal neuro exam, abnormal movements, or a clinically suspected seizure
EEG (only if a seizure is genuinely suspected — not routine). Neuroimaging (non-contrast head CT if acute concern, otherwise MRI) if the exam is focal or events recur.
Bruising, other injury, retinal findings, inconsistent history, or social concern
Non-accidental-trauma workup: neuroimaging, skeletal survey, ophthalmology, and child-protection involvement. This is the diagnosis not to miss.
Toxic exposure suspected (medications in the home, illicit substances)
Targeted toxicology / urine drug screen; involve poison control.

body.text: NOT recommended routinely (low yield, drive them by a specific finding only): CBC, electrolytes/glucose/bicarbonate, blood gas, ammonia, lactate, urine organic acids and other metabolic studies, chest radiograph, echocardiography, polysomnography, home apnea monitors, and empiric anti-reflux therapy.

Disposition: for a higher-risk infant, a brief hospitalization (typically ≤ 24 h) with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is reasonable — most strongly for age < 2 months, recurrent or clustered events, or an event that required CPR. Use shared decision-making, arrange caregiver CPR training, and ensure close follow-up. Escalate to a full workup and admission whenever the exam is abnormal or events recur in the department.

buildNote: Higher-risk branch built 2026-09-07 from the 2019 framework (Merritt et al.) + AAP 2016 — it is expert consensus, not a validated rule, and is framed that way in the module. The lower-risk pathway still matches AAP 2016 exactly. The interactive all-must-be-true lower-risk checklist is `brue-lower-risk-criteria`.
